Candidate sampling changes the evaluation task and interacts with popularity bias; lexical difficulty should therefore be interpreted conditionally on the candidate construction, rather than as full-catalog performance ([Ihemelandu & Ekstrand, 2023](https://mdw.ekstrandom.net/pubs/wi-sampled-eval)). Applying matching principles suggests: construct lexical candidates from available titles/descriptions, then draw equally sized random controls from the same user-eligible catalog, matching training-only item frequency. Equal counts in coarse frequency bins leave within-bin imbalance; use exact-frequency matching where feasible, or nearest-neighbor matching with a prespecified caliper on log(1+frequency). Restrict comparisons to common support, report unmatched candidates and exclusions, and acknowledge that trimming changes the population being evaluated ([Stuart, 2010](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2943670/)). These are methodological adaptations, not a standardized lexical-candidate protocol.

Deduplicate within each set. Across-set overlap is a separate design choice: allowing overlap estimates lexical selection versus unrestricted matched random sampling; excluding lexical candidates estimates lexical versus nonlexical alternatives and can reduce common support. Report intersection size/Jaccard overlap and analyze differences paired by user. For missing metadata, use the same metadata-eligible pool in both arms and report coverage; treat metadata-missing items separately rather than assigning empty text a meaningful similarity score. Check balance before/after matching, within category and user: raw/log-frequency standardized differences, variance ratios, quantiles, ECDF plots, text length and metadata availability; report lexical similarity as the intended contrast. Mean balance alone is insufficient, and nonsignificant balance tests do not establish equivalence ([Austin, 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3472075/)). Residual popularity or metadata imbalance limits attribution of any performance gap specifically to lexical difficulty.
